articles.title: Durga Puja 2026 start and end date: All you need to know history and Significance of Durga Puja
articles.summary: Every year, as the monsoon clouds clear and a soft chill enters the evening air, it all begins to feel different.
articles.body: Every year, as the monsoon clouds clear and a soft chill enters the evening air, it all begins to feel different. White kaash flowers sway by the roadside, the sound of the dhak starts echoing in the distance, and all of it seems to hum with one thought that Maa is coming home.For millions of people, Durga Puja is far more than a religious ritual. It is the time when families return to their hometowns, friends walk from one pandal to another late into the night, and even the busiest city slows down to make space for art, music, and food. Streets glow with lights, craftsmen see months of work come to life, and strangers greet each other with a smile.The Pooja season is here and many people are asking the same simple questions.That what arethe exact dates of the pooja, when does it begin? When does it end? What is the right time for the special rituals?Here is everything you need to know.Durga Puja 2026 start and end dateThe festival quietly began on Mahalaya itself which marks the end of Pitri Paksha and the beginning of Devi Paksha, signaling the arrival of Goddess Durga ahead of Durga Puja.According to Drikpanchang, Durga Puja 2026 begins with Maha Shashthi on Friday, October 16, and ends with Bijoya Dashami on Wednesday, October 21. Maha Ashtami, one of the most important days, falls on Monday, October 19.Here is a list to follow:Mahalaya: Saturday, October 10Maha Shashthi: Friday, October 16Maha Saptami: Sunday, October 18Maha Ashtami: Monday, October 19Maha Navami: Tuesday, October 20Vijaya Dashami: Wednesday, October 21Sandhi Puja timingsSandhi Puja will take place on Monday, October 19, from 10:27 AM to 11:15 AM. The ritual marks the meeting point of the last 24 minutes of Ashtami and the first 24 minutes of Navami. In Hindu tradition, this moment is linked to Goddess Chamunda defeating the demons Chanda and Munda. Many puja committees mark it with lamps, offerings, and special dhak performances.How is the festival celebrated from Shashthi to DashamiThe festival season actually starts earlier on Mahalaya, which fell on October 10 this year, marking the end of Pitri Paksha and the start of Devi Paksha. On Shashthi, the goddess is welcomed with rituals such as Kalparambha and Bodhan, and the evening is especially important because it marks her awakening.Saptami brings Nabapatrika Snan, when nine plants are bathed and worshipped. On Ashtami, devotees offer flowers in Pushpanjali, and many pandals also hold Kumari Puja, where a young girl is worshipped as the divine feminine. Navami closes the main worship, with bhog, dhak beats, and Dhunuchi Naach. On Dashami, married women play Sindoor Khela before the idols are immersed.Why is the festival celebrated?Durga Puja celebrates the goddess’s victory over Mahishasura, the buffalo demon. The legend is read as the triumph of good over evil, with Durga as Shakti, the divine feminine power.The festival is seen as a daughter’s homecomingDurga Puja has a deeply emotional side in Bengali culture. Maa Durga is often seen as a daughter returning to her parental home, visiting her mother and family for a few days before going back to her husband’s home on Mount Kailash. That is why the final farewell feels so personal. For many, Dashami is both a celebration and a goodbye, with people exchanging Bijoya greetings, seeking elders’ blessings, and hoping she returns next year.The festival is especially celebrated with immense fervour in BengalDurga Puja is far more than temple worship. Kolkata’s celebrations bring together idol-making, pandal architecture, lighting, music, traditional drumming, food and community participation. In December 2021, UNESCO added “Durga Puja in Kolkata” to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.UNESCO describes it as a strong example of religion and art coming together in public, with large installations and Bengali drumming, and says the divides of class, religion and ethnicity fade as crowds walk around to admire the pandals. Artists, craftsmen, designers, and local communities all play a part.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Why Asim Munir's plan to 'split' up Pakistan may spell the end of civilian govt
articles.summary: In Pakistan, the prime minister has the title, the president has the office, but the military chief has the power.
articles.body: In Pakistan, the prime minister has the title, the president has the office, but the military chief has the power. Now, field marshal Asim Munir, the country's most powerful man, is reportedly considering a way to redraw Pakistan's political map.According to The Economist, Munir is considering a radical solution to Pakistan's governance problems: Breaking up the country's four provinces into 12 to 15 smaller provinces, or possibly reorganising administration into as many as 160 smaller units.Smaller units, according to the argument for restructuring, would be easier to govern. But in a country where the military has long wielded influence over civilian governments, the political question is whether they would also be easier to control.The proposal has also raised concerns that weakening provincial governments could shift more political influence from Islamabad's civilian leadership towards the military establishment in Rawalpindi.However, the plan remains unconfirmed, and its details are unclear. But dividing Punjab and Sindh, strongholds of powerful political dynasties, could weaken established parties.Restructuring Pakistan's political map could also change who controls the country's mineral wealth and other natural resources.The Economist has raised the possibility that the proposal could become a 'divide and rule' exercise, weakening regional power centres and making them easier for the military-backed federal government to manage.Pakistan's population and resources are unevenly distributed, and many regions remain poorly served by their governments.Smaller administrative units could bring officials closer to citizens, improve public services and give neglected areas a stronger political voice.The question is whether the changes would make government more accountable to ordinary Pakistanis or concentrate more power in the hands of Munir and the military establishment.The divide-and-rule calculationPakistan's four provinces are Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Balochistan. Each has its own elected assembly and provincial government, giving regional parties an institutional base from which to challenge decisions taken by the federal government.Their populations vary sharply. According to the 2023 census, Punjab has around 128 million people, slightly more than half of Pakistan's population, while Balochistan has approximately 15 million, or about 6% of the national total.Punjab's size makes administration difficult, and residents in remote rural areas can spend hours travelling to government offices to settle land disputes or access basic services.But dividing the provinces would have political consequences as well. Large provinces can sustain powerful leaders, substantial bureaucracies and networks of elected representatives with influence beyond individual districts. Breaking them into smaller units could fragment that influence.The military establishment could then be dealing with a greater number of provincial leaders, each with a smaller political base and potentially fewer resources to challenge decisions made in Islamabad.The outcome would not necessarily favour the centre in every case. New provinces could give regional leaders and communities that feel excluded from existing political networks a stronger voice. Much would depend on the powers, funding and autonomy granted to the new administrations.Still, the proposal raises a difficult question: Is Pakistan considering smaller provinces because its existing ones are too large to govern effectively, or because some have become too politically powerful to manage easily?Punjab and Sindh: The biggest political stakesPunjab and Sindh are likely to be at the centre of any serious attempt to redraw Pakistan's provincial map. Both are major political strongholds, and dividing them could change the country's balance of power.Punjab is the main base of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), associated with the Sharif family.Nawaz Sharif has served as prime minister, his brother Shehbaz Sharif currently heads the federal government, and Nawaz's daughter Maryam Nawaz is Punjab's chief minister. The family and its party have dominated provincial politics for much of the past four decades.One longstanding proposal is to create a separate South Punjab province. Supporters argue that the region has not received adequate political representation or public investment compared with more developed parts of Punjab. A separate province could focus more directly on local infrastructure, education, healthcare and employment.But dividing Punjab could also break up the Sharif family-led PML-N's large electoral and organisational base, creating new political battlegrounds for regional parties and local leaders.Sindh presents a different challenge. It is the principal stronghold of the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), whose political roots go back to Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. The party has remained under the influence of his family, including his daughter Benazir Bhutto's widower, Asif Ali Zardari, now Pakistan's president, and their son and party chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari.Karachi, the country's commercial capital, is also in Sindh and central to its economic and political importance. For the PPP, dividing the province could weaken its established networks.For many Sindhi groups, however, the issue goes beyond party politics: Sindh represents a distinct historical, cultural and linguistic identity.Opposition to the proposal is already clear. On September 4, the Sindh assembly passed a resolution rejecting attempts to divide the province or create administrative units that would alter its boundaries. Chief minister Syed Murad Ali Shah said there would be no compromise on Sindh's geographical unity, Dawn reported.Resistance continued in October. According to Dawn, a multiparty conference held on October 11, attended by representatives of the PPP, PML-N and other political groups, resolved to oppose attempts to create new provinces or administrative units in Sindh.Any attempt to divide the province could therefore trigger a wider confrontation over political power, identity and provincial autonomy.The mineral wealth behind the debatePakistan's natural resources add another dimension to the proposed restructuring.Balochistan has deposits of copper, gold, chromite, coal and iron ore. Sindh has coal, limestone, silica sand and other industrial minerals, while KP has gemstones, marble, granite, gypsum and other deposits. Punjab is known for rock salt, iron ore, limestone and fire clay. PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan and other areas of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir also have deposits of precious and semi-precious stones and other minerals.These resources have long been at the centre of disputes over mining rights, royalties, investment and the distribution of economic benefits. Provincial governments and local communities have sought a greater say in decisions affecting their land and livelihoods.The proposed restructuring has also raised concerns that weakening provincial governments could give the military-backed federal establishment greater freedom to pursue mineral extraction projects in resource-rich regions without facing the same level of resistance from local authorities.These concerns have not been independently established as Munir's motives. Nor has a detailed plan been made public showing how a new provincial structure would change control over minerals or the distribution of revenues.The concern, however, is clear. A provincial government can negotiate with Islamabad over mining projects, royalties and development spending. A smaller unit with limited revenue and greater dependence on federal funding could find it harder to resist pressure from the centre.Balochistan illustrates the sensitivity of the issue, with long-running disputes over who benefits from the province's mineral wealth and how much local communities gain from projects in their region.Mineral extraction and investment are not, by themselves, evidence of a political power grab. The key question is whether decisions would be made transparently, with meaningful local participation, or imposed by a powerful centre with limited accountability.Why Khyber Pakhtunkhwa could be a test caseDevelopments in Imran Khan's party stronghold Khyber Pakhtunkhwa have added to concerns about the military's influence over provincial affairs.On October 11, President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency in the province, imposing Governor's rule and effectively suspending the elected government led by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party founded by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan.The Shehbaz Sharif-led government cited rising militant violence and the provincial administration's alleged failure to control the security situation.Imran-led PTI rejected the move, calling it an attack on its political stronghold and accusing the federal establishment of undermining an elected government.Reuters reported that the emergency was accompanied by the appointment of a new governor and the deployment of troops, amid political tensions over a planned march to Islamabad demanding Khan's release. PTI has denied supporting militancy and disputed the Sharif government's account of its handling of the security situation.KP is a key centre of PTI's political influence. Suspending its government has changed the balance between Khan's party and the Islamabad administration.Imran Khan's prolonged imprisonment and the imposition of emergency rule in KP could also be viewed in the context of Asim Munir's long-standing tensions with the former prime minister, who also led Pakistan to its Cricket World Cup victory.However, the emergency does not establish that Munir intends to divide KP or use it as a model for restructuring other provinces. It has nevertheless raised concerns about the federal government's ability to override elected provincial authorities, including in decisions affecting resource-rich regions.Similar concerns have been raised about the possibility of greater federal intervention in Balochistan and Sindh. But there is no established evidence of a coordinated plan to impose such measures across provinces.Is Pakistan's provincial system failing?The argument for smaller provinces has a basis in the governance challenges Pakistan faces. Its population has grown substantially since 1947, while the current four-province structure has remained in place since 1970. Administering a province as populous as Punjab is a major task, particularly when public services remain inadequate in many areas.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi has argued that the country's governance system has "collapsed" and that the existing structure cannot adequately manage population growth, debt and other pressures. He has called for smaller administrative units as part of wider reforms.But new boundaries alone would not solve corruption, weak public services or economic mismanagement. Smaller provinces would need their own institutions, budgets and administrative staff. Without adequate funding and clear powers, creating new units could increase the cost of government without improving people's lives.The military's own role in Pakistan's governance problems is also part of this debate. The country has spent long periods under direct army rule, and the armed forces continue to wield considerable influence over security and foreign policy, even under civilian governments.In recent months, Munir has wielded extraordinary power, from visiting Washington and cultivating ties with Donald Trump to earning the US president's "favourite field marshal" label and attempting to broker a deal over the Iran war.Under his tenure, Pakistan's army chief has expanded his influence well beyond military affairs, playing an increasingly prominent role in the country's foreign policy.The Economist has argued that the military cannot be separated from Pakistan's governance problems, pointing to its share of public resources, landholdings and commercial interests, as well as its influence over civilian administrations.Pakistan's economic difficulties have several causes, including debt, inflation, weak investment and structural problems in public finances. But the military's political and economic position remains a central issue in debates over accountability and the allocation of resources.Munir's authority has grown against this backdrop. Reuters reported on October 8 that the military had taken on a larger role in foreign and defence policy, including a decision to deploy additional troops to Saudi Arabia under a defence arrangement without parliamentary approval.If provincial governments are weakened while the military's influence grows, critics fear there could be fewer institutions capable of challenging decisions made by the centre. At the same time, smaller provinces could create opportunities for new regional leaders, depending on how much independence they are given.The key issue is not simply the size of the provinces, but who would control their budgets, appointments and natural resources after any restructuring.Can Munir get the plan through?Even if the military and civilian leadership agree on restructuring, Pakistan's Constitution presents a major hurdle.Article 239 requires a constitutional amendment to secure a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each house of parliament. If an amendment changes a province's boundaries, it must also be approved by the concerned provincial assembly by at least two-thirds of its total membership before it can be presented to the president for assent.That makes dividing Punjab or Sindh politically difficult. The PML-N may have reasons to consider a separate South Punjab province, but splitting Punjab could weaken the Sharif family's political base.The PPP, meanwhile, has repeatedly rejected proposals to divide Sindh, its strongest provincial stronghold.The Sindh assembly's September resolution and the multiparty conference reported by Dawn in October show that opposition extends beyond a single party. Any attempt to alter the province's boundaries without political consensus could provoke a wider confrontation.Balochistan remains a major challenge for the Sharif-Munir duo, with separatist sentiment, demands for greater autonomy and sustained militant activity complicating Islamabad's efforts to assert control over the province.Senator and former Imran Khan ally Faisal Vawda has suggested, in reporting by The Economist, that a referendum could be held in the coming months. But such a proposal raises questions about the legal process and whether a referendum could replace the constitutionally required approvals.There is also a distinction between creating 12 to 15 provinces and establishing as many as 160 administrative units.The first would fundamentally change Pakistan's federal structure. The second could involve districts or other administrative divisions, depending on their legal status and powers.Until a detailed plan is announced, it remains unclear which model is actually being considered.What happens next?Pakistan's debate over new provinces brings together several long-running disputes: The balance between civilian and military power, the influence of regional political dynasties, and control over natural resources.Supporters argue that smaller provinces could improve governance and give neglected regions a stronger voice. Critics fear that dividing established political strongholds would weaken regional parties and leave provincial governments more dependent on Islamabad.The constitutional hurdles are substantial, and opposition in Sindh is already organised. Developments in KP have added to concerns about the centre's willingness to override provincial authority in the name of security.Pakistan faces serious governance challenges, but whether redrawing its map would address them is another matter. Smaller provinces could help address regional inequalities if they receive adequate resources, meaningful autonomy and accountable institutions.If the changes instead weaken elected governments while concentrating control over funding and natural resources in the centre, the promised benefits may never reach ordinary citizens.You use AI every day. articles.title: Community pantry opens as report says 47,500 households in negative budget
articles.summary: An estimated 47,500 people in Sheffield are unable to make ends meet and pay their bills.
articles.body:
Almost 50,000 households in Sheffield are struggling to make ends meet and cannot pay their bills, according to a new cost of living report by the council.

Described as having a "negative budget", these people are unable to afford the necessary costs even after all benefit entitlements have been claimed and their outgoings have been reduced to the bare essentials.

In the same week the report was published, a new food pantry opened in the Woodseats area of the city, offering low priced food for anyone struggling with the cost of living.

Within the first hour 14 people called in, with 37-year-old Sara Ody among those through the door.

"There's always a thought process, 'can we afford this? do we have to sacrifice this to be able to afford food, childcare and clothes?' It's definitely tough," she said.

The Community Grocery pantry, run in partnership by The Message Trust and Ikon Church at Woodseats, offers membership for £1 per year, with food and household staples from just 50p.

Sara said her finances were especially tight now she is on maternity leave from work.

"There's four of us now, and I've got to the point in my maternity leave where there is not really any money coming in, so it's definitely tight trying to budget, especially in the run up to Christmas," she said.

"It's frustrating because I saved up so much money while I was working to be able to still have opportunities and do things while on maternity leave, but you have to budget all the time.

"We're finding food is so expensive and every week it seems the prices are going up and up so things like this are amazing. We can get definitely some staple bits to see us through winter."

According to the report to Sheffield City Council , Citizens Advice estimates 47,500 people in Sheffield have negative budgets.

It says that poverty in the city predates the cost-of-living crisis and reflects longer-term inequalities in income, employment, health, housing and opportunity.

However, it says years of financial pressure have also left some households with depleted savings, debt and arrears, reducing their ability to absorb further shocks

It adds that children are particularly affected, with approximately one in three children in Sheffield living in poverty, "substantially above" the national rate.

John Lawson is the regional lead for The Message Trust, which has 35 stores nationwide, and is based in Sheffield.

He says community grocery stores can bridge the gap between food banks and supermarkets, as they offer a variety of food but at a fraction of the cost.

"We opened here after seeing the need on the doorstep and the challenges that people are facing with the cost of living," he said.

"Even a lot of the community who wouldn't necessarily have been struggling five years ago are now finding themselves living paycheck to paycheck."

The store is open to everyone and there is no means testing.

Lawson added: "We want to make it accessible for everyone, so if someone is passionate about saving food from landfill, they should shop here. If someone's in crisis and needs free food, they can come here.

"Or if someone just wants to be in the community, in an amazing space like we've got here, they can come and hang out.

"We want to create an opportunity and a resource where anyone can come and access healthy food and wraparound care so we can holistically look after the whole person with mental health support, debt advice, cookery courses or just simply offering a social space for people to come together."

Another customer Debbie Schofield, 44, said she thought the pantry would help people realise they are not alone.

"I think Woodseats needs this community hub where people can get some cheaper resources and have a chat somewhere warm," she said.

"I like the concept of the community pantry. I think everybody's struggling with the cost of living, everything has gone up quite considerably, but I also feel like social media isolates us in our own homes.

"I don't feel there's a sense of community like when I was growing up, like in the 1980s and 90s. It's really important for these pantries to exist because they bring neighbours together and then people in the wider community start to recognise each other."

articles.title: Psychology says people who rehearse what to say before making a phone call may be doing it for a reason
articles.summary: You need to call your doctor to book an appointment, ask a colleague for an update or speak to a customer care executive.
articles.body: You need to call your doctor to book an appointment, ask a colleague for an update or speak to a customer care executive. Before dialling, you mentally practise the first sentence. You think about what the other person might ask, how you should respond and how to end the conversation without making it awkward. Sometimes, you rehearse the same opening line several times before finally pressing the call button. For some people, this is simply a way to organise their thoughts. For others, it may reflect discomfort with unpredictable conversations, a fear of being misunderstood or concern about how they will come across. The reasons can vary, and rehearsing a phone call does not automatically mean someone is anxious.They may want to feel prepared for an unpredictable conversationUnlike a text message, a phone call gives you little time to edit your words. The other person can interrupt, ask an unexpected question or respond in a way you did not anticipate. You have to listen and think of an answer at the same time. Rehearsing can make the conversation feel more manageable. A person might prepare the main point they want to communicate, keep important details in mind or practise how to ask a difficult question.Research has identified telephone anxiety as a form of communication apprehension. A 1990 study published in Management Communication Quarterly developed and tested a measure of telephone apprehension across five studies. The researchers examined how discomfort about telephone communication related to people's phone use. The research established that anxiety about phone calls could be studied as a distinct communication-related concern. However, preparation and anxiety are not the same thing. Someone may rehearse because they want to be clear and efficient, especially when discussing work, money or a personal matter.They may worry about saying the wrong thingSome people are less concerned about what they need to say than about how the other person will interpret it. They may worry about sounding rude, asking a foolish question, forgetting an important detail or being unable to respond quickly. This can be particularly noticeable when calling a senior colleague, speaking to someone they do not know well or raising an uncomfortable subject.A 2023 study published in Communication Research Reports, examined factors associated with anxiety about telephone conversations. The researchers found a positive relationship between digital communication use and telephone anxiety. This relationship was stronger among people who were not native speakers of English. The study also found that telephone anxiety was associated with a preference for other forms of communication. The findings suggest that comfort with phone calls can be influenced by communication habits and language-related concerns. Someone who is confident expressing themselves through messages may feel less prepared when they have to respond instantly in a conversation. That does not mean everyone who prefers texting is socially anxious. It simply shows that different communication formats can feel easier or harder for different people.Rehearsing can sometimes make the anxiety worsePreparing a few points before a call can be useful. But repeatedly imagining how the conversation might go can also create more opportunities to worry. A person may begin by practising one sentence and then start thinking about everything that could go wrong. What if the other person sounds irritated? What if they ask something unexpected? What if there is an awkward silence? Research on anticipatory processing has explored this pattern. A 2003 paper examined how people with higher and lower levels of social anxiety thought about upcoming social situations. The researchers investigated whether these patterns of thinking could contribute to anxiety before an interaction. For example, preparing three questions before calling a doctor can make the call easier. Mentally replaying every possible response for half an hour may leave someone feeling less confident about making it.They may prefer having control over their wordsWritten communication gives people time to pause, edit and choose their words. A phone call removes some of that control because the conversation unfolds in real time. People who rehearse may therefore prefer to know how they want to begin and what information they need to share. This can be especially useful when the call involves a complaint, a request for help or a conversation they have been putting off.How to make phone calls easier without scripting every wordA few simple changes can help make calls feel less demanding.Write down the main points. Note the reason for the call and two or three details you need to remember. You do not have to prepare every sentence.Practice the opening, not the entire conversation. A simple start, such as “Hello, I’m calling to ask about my appointment,” may be enough to get things moving.Allow room for unexpected questions. You cannot predict every response. It is perfectly acceptable to say, “Let me check that,” or “Could you repeat that, please?”Notice when preparation becomes postponement. If you have the information you need but keep rehearsing, try making the call before you feel completely ready.Start with manageable calls. Making routine calls can give you opportunities to become more comfortable with the pauses, questions and small mistakes that are part of ordinary conversation.Rehearsing a phone call can reflect careful planning, a desire to communicate clearly or discomfort with unpredictable conversations. Sometimes, several of these reasons overlap. The habit alone cannot tell you whether someone is shy, anxious, a perfectionist or simply organised. What matters more is how the person feels before the call and whether the preparation helps them communicate or keeps them from doing so.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: From 'Indira Gandhi' to 'PM': Cabinet approves renaming of pension schemes
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved the renaming of the National Social Assistance Programme
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved the renaming of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) and several of its sub-schemes, including those named after former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.The Cabinet also approved the continuation of NSAP for five years, from 2026-27 to 2030-31, with a total outlay of Rs 53,428 crore.Here are the approved name changes and details of the schemes:National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana. Launched on August 15, 1995, the programme provides social security assistance to poor and vulnerable households.Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Vridhavastha Pension Yojana. The scheme provides monthly financial assistance to eligible elderly people from below poverty line (BPL) households.Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Vidhawa Pension Yojana. It provides financial assistance to eligible widows from BPL households.Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana. The scheme provides monthly pension assistance to eligible persons with disabilities from BPL households.National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Parivar Labh Yojana. The scheme provides financial assistance to eligible households following the death of the primary breadwinner.Alse read: Diwali bonanza for railway staff: 78-day bonus cleared for 11.4 lakh employeesChanges to disability pensionAlongside the renaming, the Cabinet approved changes to the disability pension scheme. Monthly assistance will increase to Rs 375 for beneficiaries aged 0-79 years and Rs 625 for those aged 80 and above.The minimum benchmark disability requirement will be reduced from 80% to 40%, while the minimum age criterion will be removed, making individuals eligible for assistance from birth, subject to the scheme's other conditions.The Cabinet said the old-age and widow pension schemes, along with the family benefit scheme, would continue in their existing form.A total of 3.20 crore beneficiaries across all 36 states and Union territories are expected to benefit from the approval. Guidelines covering the revised eligibility criteria, beneficiary coverage and assistance under the disability pension scheme will be issued and implemented within three months.The programme was launched to fulfil the Central government's responsibility under Article 41 of the Constitution's Directive Principles of State Policy, which concerns public assistance in cases including old age, sickness and disability.Also read: IDBI Bank stake sale; Rs 53,428 crore welfare package- key decisions by Union cabinetGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Pope Leo spends a peaceful night in the hospital after cancer surgery
articles.summary: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV spent a calm night in the hospital after successful surgery that saw part of his right lung removed and a confirmed cancer diagnosis, the Vatican said early Wednesday.
articles.body: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV spent a calm night in the hospital after successful surgery that saw part of his right lung removed and a confirmed cancer diagnosis, the Vatican said early Wednesday. It said more information would follow later in the day. The 71-year-old American pontiff was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer that accounts for 80% of all cases, according to the American Lung Association. The 90-minute operation to remove a malignant lung nodule was completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned,” the Vatican said Tuesday. Leo was in the operating theater for nearly three hours, it said. The Vatican did not offer details on planned treatment moving forward or whether the cancer might have spread. The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer. Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli hospital as he entered Tuesday. The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began. The surgery saw the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung removed using a “video-assisted technique,” according to the Vatican. Following his surgery, the pontiff “woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor,” the Vatican said. The room is next to the usual papal apartment, complete with private chapel, which is currently undergoing renovations. This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker. The cancer diagnosis could complicate his busy schedule. Just weeks earlier, hundreds of thousands of people packed the streets of Paris for an outdoor mass on a visit that saw Leo warn about the risks of artificial intelligence. He was planning to take a historic two-week visit to South America next month, although it is unclear if that will still go ahead. Messages of support and sympathy flowed in after the news. Dr. Fernando Daniels III, a 67-year-old physician from Maryland was among many praying for Leo’s swift recovery in the Vatican’s St. Peter’s Square. “I’ve seen miracles in medicine. I’ve seen people told with terminal illnesses they wouldn’t live and they did,” he told NBC News. “Prayers of all should heal him,” said Daniels, who was traveling as part of a group. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife, Jeanette Rubio, were praying for the pope, who was born in Chicago. “May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X. “We thank God that the surgery on Pope Leo was, by all accounts, successful, and that he continues his recovery and recuperation,” New York City’s Archbishop Ronald Hicks said in a statement. German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose role is largely ceremonial, wished Leo a speedy and full recovery, the German Catholic news agency KNA reported. “The pope‘s voice on the current issues and challenges of our time is of particular importance and of value to many people worldwide, including in Germany, beyond denominational boundaries,” Steinmeier was quoted as saying. Claudio Lavanga reported from Vatican City, and Mithil Aggarwal reported from Hong Kong.

articles.title: From Elvis Presley to Where’s Waldo, four businesswomen’s scarecrow festival started in 1996 now draws 30,000 visitors to a Nova Scotia town
articles.summary: Every autumn, the seaside town of Mahone Bay in Nova Scotia turns an ordinary walk down its streets into something closer to a gallery visit, except the
articles.body: Every autumn, the seaside town of Mahone Bay in Nova Scotia turns an ordinary walk down its streets into something closer to a gallery visit, except the artworks are life-sized scarecrows posed on porches, beside shopfronts and in gardens. This year, the festival marked its thirtieth anniversary with more than two hundred and fifty handmade figures, a first-ever pottery market, glowing carved pumpkins and plenty of reasons to linger. Entry was free, the route was flat and walkable, and the experience unfolded largely outdoors. Here is how about one thousand residents built one of Nova Scotia's most-loved annual fall traditions.How four local businesswomen launched the Mahone Bay Scarecrow Festival in 1996 to bring back visitorsThe story starts in 1996, when summer ended and the visitors left with it. Sylvia Jackson of Signature Festivals of Mahone Bay told CTV News that four local businesswomen decided the town needed an event for the shoulder season, so they created a handful of scarecrows. By about the year 2000, the display had grown to between forty and fifty figures. The festival's own website describes how neighbours began hand-building life-sized scarecrows that turn porches and lampposts into a gallery, a tradition now three decades old. The festival has grown well beyond what its founders originally imagined, and that they are thrilled and still helping out. What began as a clever seasonal fix is now a genuine community landmark.Pirates, Elvis Presley, the Cat in the Hat and Where's Waldo: handmade scarecrows with pop culture flairWalking the streets meant meeting a cast of characters that kept surprising visitors. According to the festival's website, pop culture icons and original characters stood side by side, all designed and painted by artists and volunteers who spent hours sewing, painting and constructing them. Jackson told CTV News that this year's creations included scarecrow pirates, Elvis Presley, King Charles and the Cat in the Hat, along with a special pop culture feature. Where's Waldo was somewhere in town and was moved every day, reportedly making him a favourite thing to find. Many installations were staged as vignettes, so the festival felt less like a parade and more like an open-air gallery where porches, lampposts and shopfronts acted as frames. Many new artists took part this year.Beyond scarecrows: Pumpkin Patch Gallery, Nova Scotia Pottery Market, pie baking contest and quilt showScarecrows anchored the festival, yet the calendar around them was packed. The festival's website listed a Pumpkin Patch Gallery in Jubilee Park, where more than one hundred artfully carved pumpkins glowed at dusk, along with a quilt show and sale, a giant book sale, live music and children's crafts. The first-ever Nova Scotia Pottery Market took place on Sunday, October 4, with more than twenty-five ceramic artists from across the Maritimes. A fourth annual fruit pie baking contest offered cash prizes and celebrity judges, and the Shantymen of Mahone Bay sang traditional sea shanties at the bandstand. Family activities included building toy boats to float in a portable pond and an Eye Spy trail through Jubilee Woods. Most of these events were free, though the quilt show, pie sale and luncheons carried ticket prices.Why about 30,000 visitors flocked to a town of roughly 1,000 people during the busiest weeks of the festivalNumbers showed how far the idea had travelled. More than 250 handmade creations spread across town, and that the event drew an estimated 30,000 visitors at its peak into a community of about 1,000 residents. The festival's website called it a marquee shoulder season event, handmade, neighbourly and free for everyone, and described the organization behind it as a volunteer-run non-profit. The festival invited everyone to walk through town, explore the shops and vignettes, and get their picture taken with wonderful creations, noting that many were set up for "Instagram-worthy photos." The festival's website added that the event kept the steady summer flow of visitors going a little longer.Free entry, flat streets and early arrivals, how visitors explored the Mahone Bay scarecrow routeVisiting was refreshingly simple. According to the festival's website, wandering among the scarecrows cost nothing, though donations were welcome, and the displays stayed up for the entire festival window, which ran from September 25 to October 12. Weekends were liveliest, with markets and activities, while weekdays offered a quieter stroll. The route was a gentle, flat walk through the town centre, free street and lot parking was available around the waterfront, and the site advised arriving early on weekends because the town filled up fast. Well-behaved, leashed dogs were welcome outdoors, and the festival described itself as very family-friendly.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Washington girls walk off cross country meet in protest of male athlete, parents reveal how it came to this
articles.summary: Holly Burns and teammates walked off a Washington cross-country race rather than compete against an athlete who switched from the boys' team.
articles.body: Holly Burns and about a dozen other girls walked away from a cross-country race in Washington on Tuesday. They refused to compete against a male athlete who had started the season racing on the boys’ team. When the race began, half of the girls competing, and the male athlete, took off running. Burns and the other half of the girls slowly walked forward past the starting line, and then into the nearby tree line, sacrificing one of their high school competitions. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Footage of the protest has since gone viral across social media, igniting widespread awareness for one of the trans athlete incidents currently plaguing Washington state. For Burns, a Camas High School runner, the decision to protest was reinforced by strength in numbers. Her parents, Kevin and Sarah Burns, told OutKick their daughter initially wanted to avoid "making waves." "She wanted to kind of play it safe, so we, we weren't going to push it. We just kind of let her kind of feel it out. We told her that. We supported her whichever decision she tries to make," Kevins said. DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER But then her teammates began talking. The girls shared their concerns. They decided to act together. And her parents backed her. "The more I heard about her friends wanting to do something, the more I heard about her team wanting to do something, we definitely were in support of that," Kevin said. "We told her, do what you think is best." The Oct. 13 meet pitted Camas against Battle Ground. Camas hosted the event at the Underwriters Lab campus, where the girls’ race was scheduled for 4 p.m. The Burnses said they learned about the athlete’s move to girls’ competition recently. They worried about what it would mean for their daughter and her teammates. "You hear about it, but you just never think it’s going to be on your kid’s small cross-country team," Sarah said. ATTORNEY FOR ALLEGED VICTIM OF TRANS ATHLETE SEXUAL ASSAULT SAYS SCOTUS FIGHT CAN HELP SET TITLE IX PRECEDENT Camas School District has said it follows Washington law and Washington Interscholastic Activities Association eligibility rules. For the Burnses, that policy leaves their daughter’s concerns unresolved. "I don’t see how it’s OK to discriminate against my daughter and the daughters of everyone else that is trying to fairly compete," Kevin said. Their own protest began before the girls walked off. FEMALE ATHLETES, WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATES SPEAK ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRANS ATHLETE ISSUE HOVERS OVER MIDTERMS They arrived with signs, and security challenged them, the parents said. "They said that we’re not allowed to hold up signs at this event today," Kevin Burns said. "I questioned them if that was constitutionally legal, if we could express ourselves by just holding a sign. And we kind of went back and forth about public versus private property. And in the end, it didn’t seem like they really had a grasp on what they could tell us to do or not. "So I just went ahead and held up my sign, and they had several security guards following me and pestering me and telling me that I would have to leave. And I just said, no, I’m not going to leave." Other parents approached, they said. Some offered support. Others said they agreed but feared the backlash that could follow speaking publicly. At one point, Sarah said she had a confrontation with a woman who identified herself as a psychiatric nurse. "I had a lady that came up to me and said she was a psychiatric nurse and that I was a disgusting human for holding up this sign and that I was doing psychological damage to these children," Sarah said. "I told her that one day I’m gonna have to stand before my Lord and Savior and I’m gonna feel good about this." The Burnses said they respected the girls who chose to race Tuesday. They believed some wanted to preserve their chances of competing in postseason meets. "I think they all have to make their own decision," they said. For Holly, they do not yet know what sitting out will mean. "Well, we don’t know that yet," they said when asked whether the protest cost her a chance at something she had worked toward. "But there’s cost to everything when you stand up for what you believe is right, I think. If there wasn’t, then you’re not really standing up for anything," they said. "Her goal this season was just to have fun and compete and do the best that she could." Now her parents hope she can keep pursuing those goals while standing alongside her teammates. More races remain. Camas lists its next championship meet for Oct. 21 at Lewisville Regional Park. Another decision awaits Washington voters on Nov. 3. Initiative 638 would prohibit students it defines as biologically male from competing in certain female-only interschool athletic competitions. It would require students seeking to enter those competitions to provide verification of biological sex from a healthcare provider. The Burnses support the measure. But even if voters approve it, the measure would take effect 30 days after the election. Washington’s state cross-country championships are scheduled for Nov. 7. The athlete at the center of the dispute had already competed in several girls’ races. On Sept. 5, the runner finished 76th in a boys’ junior varsity race at the Ultimook meet in Oregon. By Sept. 15, the runner was competing in the girls’ race at a Camas meet involving Skyview. The Burnses had not spoken with the athlete or the athlete’s family. Their position, they said, was that the runner should compete with boys. "Their child has every right to participate in the boys athletics, just like they did at the beginning of the season, but it’s not fair to the girls," they said during the interview. Holly’s parents rejected the idea that the stakes become insignificant because the athletes are in high school. "Some of these girls work really hard to compete. It’s most of what they do all summer long. It means a lot to them," they said. They argued that losing opportunities can undo the rewards of that effort. "Then that’s devastating to all the hard work. It erases everything they’ve done." The dispute unfolds against a broader conflict over Washington’s eligibility policies. President Donald Trump’s Feb. 5, 2025, executive order directed federal agencies to protect female athletic opportunities and prioritize Title IX enforcement against federally funded institutions that require female athletes to compete against males in women’s categories. Federal officials opened an investigation into Washington’s Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction in April 2025. State Superintendent Chris Reykdal defended Washington’s protections. He said the state had allowed students to participate in athletics consistent with their gender identity since 2007 and would continue enforcing its laws unless Congress or federal courts changed the legal requirements. A separate Washington sports dispute has also reached the Supreme Court. A high school wrestler identified in court filings as K.M.K. and her mother, Stephanie Brown, have requested emergency relief, including notice and an opportunity to decline competition against male athletes without penalties. The WIAA opposed the application in a filing Tuesday, arguing that the requested relief would conflict with state law and compromise other students’ privacy. The Supreme Court’s docket showed the responses filed Tuesday and no ruling on the application. The Burnses plan to keep showing up. "So we made a few contacts and we might go forward with that and have a more organized protest the next time," Kevin said. Asked whether they would return with more signs and shirts, the answer came quickly. "Definitely. Yeah, we will." They also said they were prepared for greater national attention if it helped bring change. Some friends disagree with their position. The couple hopes those relationships can survive the dispute. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "I think we can respect each other outside of the controversy," they said. Their fears extend beyond one race. They worry about what the policy means for college athletics, Olympic competition and other spaces reserved for women. "Women’s spaces will be erased," they said. For now, their daughter has chosen to stand with her teammates. Her parents want other families to know they can speak up, too. "Don’t be afraid." "Stand up for girls’ rights." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Girls need their own space. They need their sports. They need their athletics." OutKick reached out to Camas, WIAA, Washington Superintendent for Public Instruction and Battle Ground for comment. Battle Ground hosted the race.

articles.title: Carrie depicts the devastating consequences of teen cruelty in the age of social media
articles.summary: There is a scene in Carrie—the recent TV series of Stephen King’s first book which took the world by storm 52 years ago—that is unforgettable.
articles.body: There is a scene in Carrie—the recent TV series of Stephen King’s first book which took the world by storm 52 years ago—that is unforgettable. Carrie, the sheltered and homeschooled teen, has her periods in the locker room of her high school. She doesn’t know anything about periods due to her strict religious upbringing; and the high-schoolers upon discovering go into full bully mode. They throw her in the shower, everyone throws tampons at her and there’s a mass frenzy where every girl in the women’s shower room joins in the fun – ‘Carrie Red’ they all scream as a horrified girl cowers as her kind outlook about the world is shattered just as her girlhood. It’s all recorded on social media and shared.The horror of Stephen King's Carrie has always been supernatural, but the machinery that produces her humiliation is recognizably human. That is the genius of King’s first book, which was almost not published because he threw away his pages in the dustbin. King’s wife found it, saw the potential and asked him to keep on writing. That’s why and how the world got Carrie in 1974. It became an instant bestseller. The rest is history.Cut to 2026, Flannagan’s Carrie is a scathing indictment of the times we live in. Social media is at the forefront of the horror auteur’s adaptation. He said in a recent interview to The Independent that Carrie had not dissipated over the years, but grown more relevant than ever. The abuse and violence that’s always existed in schools has in fact “metastasised” on the internet and on mobile phones. “There is something new and vital to say about being a teenager today and about the nature of cruelty and kindness,” Flannagan said.This particular adaptation poses a disturbing question about modern adolescence: What happens when teenage cruelty becomes a collective sport? What happens when humiliation becomes social currency, and the person everyone targets is pushed beyond the limits of what they can bear?Because the troubling thing about teenage cruelty is that it rarely announces itself as cruelty. It arrives often disguised as a joke or a nickname. Sometimes, a meme, an exclusive group chat, or a video shared simply because everyone else is laughing.Adolescents have always policed one another's looks, clothes, bodies, social standing, and romantic desirability. But the culture in which they do this has fundamentally changed. Humiliation can now be recorded, replayed, circulated, and preserved long after the school day is over. The audience is no longer confined to the classroom or the corridor.This dynamic presents a picture far more compelling than the familiar argument that social media has simply made teenagers meaner. It says emphatically that modern digital culture rewards cruelty with attention, belonging, and status.Humiliation as currency and reward The transformation of teenage conflict is rooted in how digital networks alter social incentives. In his psychological research on adolescent popularity, Dr. Mitch Prinstein, author and psychology professor, drew a clear distinction between two forms of social standing: likability and status.Likability, he said, is built on mutual trust, kindness, and making peers feel valued. Status, on the other hand, is driven by power, dominance, visibility, and social influence. And in this world where everyone is obsessed over their filtered and masked lives, status is all that matters.Psychology also says that during early adolescence, sensitivity to peer standing reaches its peak. On digital platforms, status is measured through visible metrics such as likes, shares, comments, and follower counts. In this environment, targeting an outsider often functions as social currency.Mocking or excluding a peer allows participants to signal alignment with the dominant group, earning attention and status at the victim's expense.When lines of decency disappearMany psychologists and cultural commentators have been highlighting for the past two decades that the exponential growth of online harassment has created a profound shift in moral boundaries. As cruelty is continuously replayed and gamified, standard boundaries of acceptable behaviour have disintegrated in our society.Author and journalist Jon Ronson, who has documented online public shaming, observes how peer groups establish boundaries through public destruction: “We’re defining the boundaries of normality by tearing apart the people outside of it.”When public shaming becomes a daily routine, cruelty ceases to feel extreme to those participating in it. This insensitivity is accelerated by digital detachment. It’s as if we are being cruel by posting it’s not real. It’s not tangible. There are no consequences.Furthermore, educational psychologists have pointed out that modern adolescent cruelty has grown increasingly covert and sophisticated. Journalist Rick Hampson, summarizing psychological research on modern school dynamics, wrote: “Educational psychologists describe a new kind of bullying. The perpetrators are attractive, athletic, and academically accomplished — and comfortable enough around adults to know what they can and can’t get away with in school and online. These bullies are so subtle and cunning it's hard for school staff to know if what looks like bullying really is, and what to do about it.”Because these aggressors maintain high social standing and polite relationships with adults, their cruelty goes largely unchecked. The victim's distress is written off as an overreaction, effectively normalizing mistreatment and erasing basic standards of decency within the school environment.Teen dynamics as a mirror of the adult worldThe breakdown of decency among adolescents cannot be viewed in isolation though; it directly reflects the broader adult society teenagers are inheriting. Social psychologists Jonathan Haidt and Greg Lukianoff, authors of The Coddling of the American Mind, have argued that digital communication has fostered a widespread “call-out culture” reliant on public shaming. They observed that common-enemy group dynamics create environments where “almost anything a person says or does can lead to public shaming,” instilling constant fear and forcing individuals to censor themselves.Teenagers observe adults in politics, media, and public life receiving praise, clout, and financial rewards for hostile, mocking, and exclusionary behaviour. When adult public discourse rewards humiliation over empathy, adolescents adopt the same tactics to navigate their own social hierarchies.The digital schoolyard becomes a microcosm of a hyper-competitive, outrage-driven culture where empathy is framed as weakness and hostility is accepted as a necessary tool for self-preservation.From King to Margaret AtwoodThe persistent nature of adolescent malice has long been explored by authors who examine human behavior under group pressure. In the original text of Carrie, King observed how high school bullies evolve as they enter adulthood: “People don't get better, they just get smarter. When you get smarter you don’t stop pulling the wings off flies, you just think of better reasons for doing it.”King's insight here underlines that ageing does not automatically eliminate cruelty; increased intelligence simply provides adults with sophisticated rationalizations for hurting others. This aligns with William Golding's assessment of group behavior in Lord of the Flies, where he famously noted that "man produces evil as a bee produces honey".In another classic, Cat's Eye, author Margaret Atwood presents a detailed portrait of relational aggression among young girls. Atwood illustrated how adolescent cruelty often operates under the guise of friendship and concern.The protagonist of Cat’s Eye, Elaine Risley, is systematically criticized and isolated by her close friend Cordelia. Atwood captures the psychological confusion of being targeted by peers who claim to care: “Cordelia is my friend. She likes me, she wants to help me, they all do. They are my friends... I have never had any before and I’m terrified of losing them. I want to please. Hatred would have been easier. With hatred, I would have known what to do. Hatred is clear, metallic, one-handed, unwavering; unlike love.”Dance of the macabreAtwood demonstrated that relational cruelty forces the victim to internalize the mistreatment, continually searching for personal flaws to justify the bullies’ behaviour. Over time, the line between the victim and the perpetrator becomes blurred. In Cat’s Eye, Atwood’s protagonist later reflects: “I’m not afraid of seeing Cordelia. I’m afraid of being Cordelia. Because in some way we changed places, and I’ve forgotten when’.Towards the end, as the city of Chamberlain burns we watch Carrie dancing and laughing through the road as everything around her falls apart and dies. It’s not very different from real life scenarios played all over the world around us. But the question still remains.Why? How can so much devastation feel like child’s play? Flanagan offers a simple explanation. “I think it’s simply because they haven’t lived long enough to see the consequences of that cruelty.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery was like 'advanced Alzheimer's'
articles.summary: The TV presenter says she suffered memory loss following her operation to remove a benign tumour.
articles.body:
TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery.

Speaking on Paloma Faith's podcast Mad, Sad and Bad, the 58-year-old described suffering from memory loss while recovering from an operation to remove a benign brain tumour in 2024.

"After I'd had my brain tumour taken out, I had advanced Alzheimer's, so I couldn't remember anything," the former Big Brother host told singer and Celebrity Traitors star Faith.

"When I came out of the operation, I didn't know I'd had an operation," she recalled. One regular member of staff would ask McCall every day if she could remember their name. "And I'd go, 'I don't know'."

The Masked Singer judge had surgery in November 2024 after a colloid cyst was found in a health check-up as part of her menopause advocacy work.

In November last year she revealed she had also undergone surgery for breast cancer.

She called 2025 the "hardest year" for both her and her partner.

Speaking about the recovery from her brain surgery, she said: "Michael would come and visit [hospital] for two hours, and he'd go to the loo and come back, and I'd go, 'Oh my God, you're here', and I didn't know he'd been there.

"I couldn't watch a movie for six months because I couldn't remember what had happened in the movie 15 minutes before. [When reading] a book I couldn't remember the page before."

A year ago, for the first time since the surgery, she noted, she woke up and could remember what she had done the previous day.

According to the NHS , later stage symptoms of Alzheimer's disease include "significant problems with short and long-term memory".

Alzheimer's is a progressive disease and so symptoms gradually worsen over years.

After brain surgery, though, problems tend to be worst early on, then stabilise and improve over weeks to months. Some people are left with milder lasting changes.

Music therapy can help people to recover from brain injuries and McCall said she believes it was ultimately singing lessons that had "healed" her.

In April 2025, McCall revealed she had been told - following MRI scans - that her tumour was "not coming back".

A benign tumour is not cancerous, but such cysts tend to grow slowly, according to the Brainstrust charity.

Non-cancerous brain tumours are more common in people over the age of 50, and symptoms can include headaches, vision problems and drowsiness, the NHS says.

McCall's surgery, known as a craniotomy, involved part of her skull being removed to take out the tumour.

She has spoken about the procedure and her recovery, including on her own podcast called Begin Again.

articles.title: Israeli plan to reopen settler ‘Route 463’ threatens to isolate Ramallah
articles.summary: Israeli plans to reopen Route 463 for settlers threaten to isolate Palestinian villages and fragment Ramallah.
articles.body:
The Israeli army is reportedly preparing to reopen Route 463 to settler traffic, a move that threatens to isolate eight Palestinian villages and two large residential neighbourhoods in the occupied West Bank.

The areas that would be most affected by the reopening of the road would be northern Ramallah and el-Bireh, a suburb of Ramallah city. It would separate the northern and southern parts of the Ramallah and el-Bireh Governorate.

The road extends for about 10km (6 miles) from el-Bireh and the Jalazone refugee camp in the east to Ein Qiniya in the west.

It was originally constructed in the mid-1990s to connect the Beit El settlement, north of Ramallah, to Dolev, another settlement to the west of the city.

Following the outbreak of the Second Intifada in 2000, the Israeli army barred both settlers and Palestinians from using the road for a period.

The reopening of the road is part of a 1.075-billion-Israeli-shekel ($355m) settler infrastructure budget, aimed at connecting settlements in the occupied West Bank, illegal under international law.

While there is no timeline for the reopening of Route 463, the far-right Israeli government is pushing for it to be implemented before Israeli elections on October 27 . The law will bypass the Knesset in an apparent attempt to speed up the process.

The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, a monitor affiliated with the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), warned that the plan falls under a “systematic policy to dismantle Palestinian geographic and demographic contiguity” in a governorate home to nearly 400,000 Palestinians across 80 communities.

If reopened, tens of thousands of Palestinians would be forced to use an old alternative road near the Jalazone camp, north of Beit El, which is already heavily congested and would be unable to accommodate any increase in traffic.

Jamal Juma, coordinator of the Popular Campaign to Resist the Wall and Settlements, a coalition of independent Palestinian civil society groups, said the reopening of the road will completely encircle the western side of Ramallah.

The villages affected will include Surda, at-Tira, and Wadi at-Tira to the north of Ramallah, and Ein Qiniya, Ras Karkar, Deir Ibzi, and Ein Arik to the west. The impacted zone would extend southwest to Beitunia and the Fruits Roundabout, southwest of Ramallah, connecting to the town of Safa and Route 443, a main artery between Jerusalem and Israel.

Road closures to the east have pushed the urban expansion of Ramallah, the administrative capital of Palestine, westwards over the past two decades, making one continuous urban block between the city and neighbouring areas such as Birzeit and Surda. Opening the road to settlers will impede this expansion, separating Ramallah from its surrounding villages.

Turning a route used by the inhabitants of heavily populated West Bank villages into a “settler road” will likely be accompanied by more military checkpoints, watchtowers, and widespread land confiscations, Juma warned, all affecting Palestinians. There could also be more home demolitions and restricted access for farmers under the pretext of “settler security”.

Settler roads are a major component of a network that connects settlements and outposts while separating Palestinian communities. As of March 2026, settler roads occupy more than 3 percent of the occupied West Bank’s area, with many more swaths of Palestinian land affected by their presence.

The commission noted that out of 173 military and security orders issued between October 2023 and April 2026, 66 were dedicated to constructing settler roads. During the first half of 2026 alone, the Israeli occupation issued 40 military land seizure orders targeting 611 dunams – a dunam being 1,000 square metres – to build 16 security roads.

The push to reopen the road follows a wave of pogroms across the occupied West Bank by settlers, in coordination with the Israeli military.

On September 8, settlers closed a roundabout near Ein Ayoub in the Ras Karkar area, pelting Palestinian vehicles with stones.

The attacks and the push for the reopening of the road coincide with a tightening of restrictions on Palestinian movement in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, when Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began.

Munif Treish, the mayor of el-Bireh, told Al Jazeera that 95 percent of the road’s route falls within Area B, which according to the 1995 Oslo II Accords is under Palestinian civil administration and joint Israeli and Palestinian security control. Only a small section lies in Area C, which is under full Israeli control.

Treish said the reopening of the road would be a “clear violation” of agreements Israel has previously agreed to in the past with the PLO.

“The repurposing of the street for the benefit of settlers and the military constitutes an existential threat that paralyses urban expansion and serves settlement activities, harming the future of 250,000 Palestinians,” he said.

“The municipality will not allow it to be confiscated and diverted to serve settlements and will continue to pursue all legal avenues to prevent this.”

articles.title: Death penalty for Muskan Rastogi, her lover Sahil Shukla in blue drum murder case
articles.summary: MEERUT: Exactly 15 days after a district and sessions court in Meerut convicted Muskan Rastogi and her lover Sahil Shukla of murdering Muskan’s husband,
articles.body: MEERUT: Exactly 15 days after a district and sessions court in Meerut convicted Muskan Rastogi and her lover Sahil Shukla of murdering Muskan’s husband, merchant navy officer Saurabh Rajput, dismembering his body and concealing it in a blue plastic drum filled with cement in March 2025, the court gave them capital punishment on Wednesday.The verdict came after more than 100 hearings and examination of 22 witnesses.Prosecution lawyer KK Chaubey said district and sessions judge Arvind Kumar Mishra cited Mahabharata and said that to punish the guilty in accordance with the intensity of his crime is also Dharma and hence, gave Muskan and her lover Sahil Shukla death sentence.Besides, they were fined Rs 50,000 each for the crime under IPC sec 302 (murder) and Rs 20k each for causing disappearance of evidence IPC 238 (A).Muskan and Sahil appeared before the court through video conferencing. Saurabh’s family’s lawyer Vijay Bahadur said, “We had cited three cases of the similar nature in which the courts had given death sentence.”Rajput’s mother, Renu Devi, was present at the court when the verdict was pronounced.“My son cannot come back but I had prayed every day for the last 18 months that they should be given death sentence. I am thankful to Mata Rani for hearing my prayers. I am sure, this kind of sentence will serve as a deterrence and will save many mothers from the trauma I have experienced.”How the murder unfoldedRajput, 35, had returned to Meerut from London in late February 2025 and he was killed on March 4.Police alleged that Rastogi and Shukla drugged Rajput before stabbing him to death. His body was then dismembered and the remains placed inside a drum sealed with cement.Investigators said the accused had initially considered disposing of the body in a suitcase but turned to the drum after they could not fit the remains inside it.The remains were discovered after a foul smell emanated from the drum in mid-March.Police arrested Rastogi and Shukla after they returned from a trip to Himachal Pradesh.February 24-25, 2025: Saurabh Rajput returns to Meerut from London. Muskan Rastogi’s birthday is celebrated the following day.March 4, 2025: Muskan and Sahil Shukla allegedly drug Saurabh, stab him to death and dismember his body. His remains are packed into a blue drum with cement and sand. The duo leaves for Himachal Pradesh.Mid-March 2025: Muskan allegedly tells her maternal family about the murder. A police case follows, and Saurabh’s remains are recovered from the drum on March 17.March 18, 2025: Muskan and Sahil are arrested.March 19, 2025: A court sends the duo to 14 days of judicial custody.May 12, 2025: Police file a nearly 1,000-page chargesheet, including around 34 witness statements. The charges include murder and destruction of evidence.November 24, 2025: Muskan gives birth to a girl while in custody. She and the newborn are shifted to a women’s barrack. Saurabh’s family seeks a DNA test to establish the child’s paternity.March 2025-September 2026: The trial spans around 13 months, with 22 prosecution witnesses examined.September 17, 2026: Final arguments conclude, with the prosecution seeking the death penalty for both accused.September 30, 2026: Muskan and Sahil are convicted of murder and destruction of evidence. The court fixes October 14 for sentencing.October 14, 2026: A Meerut court sentences Muskan and Sahil to death.Police filed a chargesheet running to more than 1,000 pages in May 2025. It included forensic reports, call detail records, CCTV footage and statements from people connected to the investigation.Among those whose statements were recorded were Rajput’s parents and brother, Rastogi’s parents, a cab driver, a medical store owner, sellers of the knife and drum and the cement shop owner.Investigators also recorded statements from hotel owners in Shimla, Manali and Kasauli, where the accused allegedly stayed after the killing.Police said there was no eyewitness to the murder. The prosecution relied on the evidence gathered during the investigation to establish the case against the two accused.Rajput’s mother, Renu Devi, had demanded the death penalty after the conviction. articles.title: St Mellons crash: Mechanic who falsified car MOT given community order
articles.summary: Eve Smith, Darcy Ross and Rafel Jeanne died when the car crashed into woodland in Cardiff in 2023.
articles.body:
A mechanic who gave a car a fraudulent MOT just weeks before it was involved in a fatal crash that killed three people has been given a 12-month community order.

Neil John Lewis, 47, from Cardiff, had previously pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation .

Eve Smith, 21, Darcy Ross, 21, and Rafel Jeanne, 24, died when the car crashed into woodland in St Mellons, Cardiff , in March 2023. They lay undiscovered for two days. Two other people survived.

Cardiff Magistrates' Court heard Lewis had owned G and J Motors for 21 years and had voluntarily surrendered his testing certificate following the incident.

The car had been sold at auction to a friend of victim Rafel Jeanne, who was driving on the night of the fatal crash . The car had previously been involved in a crash in Scotland.

It failed an MOT carried out on 9 February 2023 with the warning system light on, indicating a fault with the seatbelt, air bag, or both, and with the mileage recorded at about 98,000.

Lewis retested the car two weeks later, telling police in interview when he did so "the seatbelt and warning light were now off and the rear seatbelt was now working", so he "passed it with some advisories" and it was collected by Jeanne.

He sent a text starting with a grin emoji which read: "Car is done. It's 560 you have to sort the seatbelt and the airbag light. I've passed the car though."

The seatbelts on the car had not ever been replaced and were defective.

Abigail Jackson, prosecuting, said she was not asking for the fatal crash to be treated as an "aggravating" factor to the offence.

Jon Lewis, defending, said Lewis had been in the motor industry for 30 years "with no prior criticism or complaint".

He said Lewis's decision to pass the MOT was "baffling" and it was unclear why he chose to ignore the standards "that had become the very foundation of his professional business".

Judge Charlotte Murphy said choosing the "harm" levels in the case was "not straightforward", saying she was able to consider the "wider impact" of the defendant's actions.

She said his actions represented a "dereliction of his duty" as an MOT tester but she accepted it was a "one-off offence" and "not motivated by financial gain".

Lewis was ordered to do 100 hours of unpaid work, and pay a £185 court surcharge and £114 costs.

The crash involved five people - Sophie Russon, Smith, Ross, Jeanne and Shane Loughlin, 32.

They were last seen at about 02:00 GMT on 4 March 2023 following a night out.

The families of the three young women had all reported them missing on the evening of 4 March, with Gwent Police receiving the first missing persons report in relation to the group at about 19:30.

Family and friends of the five made repeated appeals to find the missing group over the course of the weekend, with the mother of one of the girls saying she had been told to stop contacting police for updates.

They were eventually found just after midnight on 6 March.

The car had crashed deep in undergrowth near a roundabout, and they were not found for 46 hours.

Smith, Jeanne and Ross died while Russon and Loughlin were critically injured and taken to hospital.

In November 2025, the IOPC said four Gwent Police officers would face gross misconduct hearings .

Family members of those involved have previously expressed their upset and frustration over delays in getting answers about what happened that night.

In July, there were angry scenes outside the court when Lewis was confronted by the family of Darcy Ross . They showed his a picture of Darcy, telling him to "remember her name".

On Wednesday, none of the victims' families attended the hearing.
