articles.title: The Nobel Peace Prize has become a fig leaf for left-wing activism
articles.summary: Alfred Nobel created an award for world peace, but Navi Pillay's selection highlights how the committee rewards progressive causes over diplomacy.
articles.body: Alfred Nobel intended the peace prize for those who had done the most to advance peace among nations. Instead, it is increasingly handed out to the international activist class: people who say the right things, back the right causes and appeal to the political instincts of a handful of parliamentarians in a rarefied progressive bubble. This year’s award to Navi Pillay is a case in point. Pillay is best known for chairing the U.N. commission of inquiry that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza. Her selection will inevitably be read as an endorsement of a U.N. culture in which hostility to Israel is not a liability but a badge of moral seriousness. NOBEL PEACE PRIZE AWARDED TO UN JURIST WHO ACCUSED ISRAEL OF COMMITTING GENOCIDE IN GAZA But there is more to Pillay’s record than the commission’s fixation on Israel. When Denmark’s embassy in Pakistan was bombed after Danish newspapers republished the Muhammad cartoons, former Foreign Minister Per Stig Møller reportedly said Pillay’s response was not to defend free speech, but to suggest censorship and restrictions on it. Her reaction to Charlie Hebdo was much the same. Pillay reportedly called the magazine "doubly irresponsible" for publishing Muhammad cartoons. She is said to have described them as "malicious and deliberately provocative" and said she "fully understands why people wish to protest strongly." When Islamists answer speech with threats, violence and murder, Pillay’s first instinct seems to be to scold those who exercised their right to speak. In 2022, she defended fellow U.N. commissioner Miloon Kothari after he referred to a "Jewish lobby" controlling social media and questioned whether Israel should even be a member of the United Nations. Kothari later apologized. An event in Pillay’s honor at Berlin City Hall was canceled after the mayor withdrew her support. WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM There are more reports of uncomfortable episodes. Pillay is said to have declined to attend the 2010 Nobel ceremony for the imprisoned Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo, citing a scheduling conflict in Geneva as Beijing pressured foreign governments to stay away. At Durban II the previous year, she remained seated while Mahmoud Ahmadinejad delivered an antisemitic tirade against Israel and Western delegations walked out. She condemned his speech later, but admitted that she had been "naive" about the Iranian president. A review of Pillay’s first two years as U.N. human-rights chief found no public statements from her on abuses in dictatorships such as Cuba, North Korea, Eritrea, Saudi Arabia, Sudan or Belarus. This is the person the Nobel Committee now presents as a model of human rights, freedom and peace. The prize has a long history of such decisions. AMBASSADOR JEFF BARTOS: UN MUST ABANDON ANTI-AMERICAN, ANTI-WESTERN LEGACY OF DURBAN CONFERENCE In 1994, Yasser Arafat was awarded the Peace Prize despite a political career built around hijackings, murder and the glorification of violence against civilians. In 1973, Henry Kissinger and North Vietnam’s Le Duc Tho received it for negotiating a Vietnam ceasefire that quickly fell apart. Tho refused the award because peace had plainly not been achieved. In 2007, the prize went to Al Gore and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Climate change may be an important issue; it is not, however, what Nobel had in mind when he wrote of peace among nations. Barack Obama received the award in 2009, less than nine months into his presidency and before any significant diplomatic achievement. Even Obama seemed embarrassed by how premature it was. The European Union won in 2012, not for a particular peace agreement or diplomatic breakthrough, but for a lofty view of Europe that appealed to the Oslo establishment. None of this is an argument against human rights, international law or humanitarian work. It is an argument against pretending that every fashionable cause belongs under the heading of furthering world peace. There is a difference between speaking the language of peace and doing the hard work of making it. The latter involves deterrence, diplomacy, compromise, alliances and often dealing with people one does not like. It is not always glamorous and rarely produces applause in international conference halls. Consider the Abraham Accords. They normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states, creating embassies, direct flights, trade, investment and security cooperation. They replaced formal hostility with working relations between governments that had long treated one another as enemies. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Some may dislike Jared Kushner or the Trump administration. That is beside the point. Kushner did more to advance peace between states than many of the campaigners and organizations celebrated by the Nobel Committee in recent years. Yet it is almost impossible to imagine the committee rewarding such an achievement. Association with Trump alone would make Kushner unacceptable to the small political circle that controls the prize. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION That is the problem. The Nobel Peace Prize is decided by five people appointed by Norway’s parliament. They have the power to pronounce who represents the world’s highest moral ideals. Too often, they use it to reward people who share their own progressive assumptions. The Stockholm-based Nobel Foundation cannot simply reclaim the prize. Nobel’s will assigns responsibility to a committee appointed by Norway’s Parliament. But the committee can be criticized, and it should no longer be treated with the automatic reverence it enjoys. Alfred Nobel created an award for exceptional achievements that furthered world peace. The Norwegian committee has turned it into an annual seal of approval for causes it happens to favor. articles.title: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
articles.summary: On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised UK plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing.
articles.body:
"Get your fiscal health in order," is a key message at the the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting here in Thailand.

The IMF is worried about the debts of the world's biggest economies. It is doing its job as a watchdog, looking for and warning about financial vulnerabilities.

In the meantime, the finance ministers of former crisis countries are boasting about how little their borrowing costs have gone up, compared to the world's biggest economies, such as the US.

On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised the UK's plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing, bucking the trend of the rest of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US.

The IMF clearly seeing the UK in a different light to these major economies is very interesting.

"The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively and we see the UK in that sense enjoying a bit of a better growth prospect," managing director Kristalina Georgieva said earlier.

Her comments followed those of the IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro who told me that UK borrowing reductions "stand out".

Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF

UK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next year

The IMF's twice-yearly assessment of global countries' economic prospects showed only the UK among the G7 having a serious plan for consolidation of its annual borrowing over the next few years, worth nearly 4% of the size of the economy. The US, Germany and Japan are increasing borrowing. Canada and Italy are keeping borrowing at the same level.

It appears the UK is now the IMF's model pupil - at the top of the G7 table for reducing deficits.

This matters because for the past half decade the UK has been on the bond market naughty step, often having the highest borrowing rates among the G7 since the Liz Truss mini budget, as political and economic crises afflicted different governments.

While this is good news for the chancellor and the Treasury, it also points to the sort of Budget we will get in a fortnight's time. To keep its plans to reduce debt on track, John Healey is likely to have limited room for extra spending. He will want to marry this with limited tax rises. There could be a modest decrease in the margin for error around meeting debt rules - so-called headroom. If so that will be tied to providing a cushion against an expected rise in energy prices due to the ongoing Middle East conflict and the impact on the cost of living overall - the so called global inflation shock.

This is likely to mean disappointment for many public services expecting cash injections to account for rising inflation, as suggested this week by think tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies. It will mean tough public sector pay discussions.

It won't be "austerity" but the chancellor is likely to lean into the IMF framing of a government with austere plans, relative to other advanced countries. The initial prize is to avoid the direct gaze of the bond markets, whose full glare is on others, such as France now. The bigger prize could be lower relative borrowing costs for government and households.

Ultimately forecasts mean nothing without the underpinning of solid plans. Those plans will be here for everyone to judge soon enough.

articles.body: A Canadian village is welcoming visitors back for a night-time attraction featuring thousands of illuminated pumpkin creations. PumpkInferno returns to Upper Canada Village in Ontario in October 2026 for its 15th season, bringing new themed displays, interactive activities and familiar favourites.According to The St. Lawrence Parks Commission, this year’s event features new exhibits inspired by jungle creatures, racing through the decades, childhood toys, and destinations across all seven continents.The outdoor experience combines intricate pumpkin artistry with family-friendly entertainment, seasonal treats, and photo opportunities. Visitors can explore the displays on selected evenings throughout October, while dedicated Accessibility Nights will provide a different way to experience the attraction.PumpkInferno returns for its 15th season with new illuminated pumpkin displaysThe 2026 season introduces new exhibits at Upper Canada Village. PKF1 takes visitors on a racing adventure through the decades, while Jungle Giants features larger-than-life creatures from the wild. Together, the themed installations form the illuminated outdoor attraction, with colourful pumpkin creations bringing different scenes to life after dark.How artists create PumpkInferno’s thousands of illuminated pumpkin displaysThe displays at PumpkInferno are made using hand-carved artificial pumpkins rather than traditional jack-o’-lanterns. articles.title: Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance: Attacks soar, oil flows crash again
articles.summary: Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been experiencing the worst spate of attacks since the start of the war.
articles.body:
Iran’s military said it has expanded its surveillance of the Strait of Hormuz by deploying new units to target ships, amid a desperate tussle between Tehran and Washington to control the waterway, among the world’s most important passages for energy transport.

With the United States naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has repeatedly said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the strait.

Tehran’s latest announcement coincides with a surge in attacks in the waterway and a fall in oil transit after crude flows had risen back to pre-war levels in September.

Chris Featherstone, a political scientist at the University of York in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera the increased attacks and their impact on energy flows demonstrate the fragility of the strait as a key pathway for oil exports.

So, what’s going on and who controls the Strait of Hormuz now?

What has Iran said about expanding its presence in Hormuz?

The navy said these units would maintain “real time surveillance of enemy activities and maritime traffic in the region”.

It also warned vessels not to switch off their transponders and urged them to coordinate with Iranian armed forces for safe passage through the area.

Separately, an Iranian official told the Reuters news agency that Tehran had started ⁠using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.

The strategy includes a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the November midterm elections in the US, according to the official.

Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been experiencing the worst spate of attacks since the start of the US and Israel’s war on Iran in late February.

According to maritime tracking firm Kpler, 10 tankers were struck in the strait between September 28 and October 4, followed by another strike on October 5.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre has separately recorded 15 other attacks between October 6 and October 14, with 11 of them occurring in just the past four days. They include a container ship and a tanker hit by unknown projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, UKMTO said.

Iran maintains that its attacks and restrictions in the waterway are a matter of national security and self-defence in response to the US-Israel war. Iranian authorities have also signalled they intend to disrupt a US-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the strait during the war.

In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) noted that the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained “severe”, the second-highest level.

Attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), “attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” JMIC said.

UAV stands for unmanned aerial vehicle, or drone, while VHF hailing refers to Iranian forces using standard marine radio to verbally contact, track, and intimidate passing merchant ships on international communication channels.

Before the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.

In retaliation for the US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait and has stepped up attacks on vessels trying to break its regulations. Meanwhile, Washington has also maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.

In September, however, Gulf oil flows through Hormuz, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, Kpler reported . Shepherded by the US Navy, more and more oil tankers had started passing through.

The Iranian threat meant ship crew were being paid hefty bonuses, insurance rates remained very high, and some analysts suspect that Gulf nations may also have been paying off Iran to allow tankers to transit. This means that while more oil was being exported from the region, crude prices remained high.

But the surge in Iranian attacks in recent days has changed the equation. According to Kpler, only 2.9 million barrels of oil were carried through the waterway on October 11, the lowest level this month. As recently as October 8, nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through the strait. The pre-war average was 17.1 million barrels a day.

Oil prices continued to climb on Wednesday morning, with Brent crude futures gaining 89 cents, or 0.8 percent, to $106.58 a barrel as of 00:30 GMT. Brent futures had closed at $105.69 a barrel on Tuesday, while West Texas Intermediate settled at $94.14.

On Wednesday, a US military official confirmed to Reuters that Iran had changed tactics in the Strait of Hormuz in one significant way.

The official noted that after Washington destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels.

The US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from dhows, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said, adding that US forces confronted one such vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) has also rejected assertions by the commander of the IRGC that Tehran controls the Strait of Hormuz and would sink approaching US warships.

“IRGC’s navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz,” CENTCOM said on X.

The military command added that US forces assisted Gulf partners to ship more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strategic chokepoint on Monday.

Since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz after the war began, the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid the energy crisis caused by Iran’s attacks on ships.

On Sunday night, Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, claimed that US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers.

He said this US shuttle system was an explicit target for Tehran, and that Iran has been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks.

“You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.

This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks.

Iran has claimed that the US accepted some of its seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and for ending the war, but that Washington’s response was “insufficient”. Tehran insists that a deal will only materialise when all its demands are met.

“The Trump administration has not moved to engage with continued negotiations, and hasn’t sought further help from potential interlocutors, such as Qatar and Pakistan,” Chris Featherstone, the University of York political scientist, said.

“For Iran, they may be seeing this as a point to increase pressure on the Trump administration.”

But he noted that the strait is not under Iranian control, and that Tehran’s attacks only attempt to show that Washington does not control the waterway either.

“As such, US allies will increase pressure for the Trump administration to bring more stability to the region, or show a path towards achieving greater stability,” he added.

articles.title: Mauritius reels from worst riots in decades after woman shot by police
articles.summary: Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam imposed a curfew after days of unrest that first began over water shortages.
articles.body:
Police in Mauritius imposed an overnight curfew overnight to quell the worst riots to break out on the Indian Ocean island in decades.

Peaceful protests over water shortages and the high cost of living that started a week ago erupted into violence on Friday when a woman was shot and wounded by police at a roadblock.

The circumstances of the shooting are not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody.

Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam ordered the curfew on Tuesday, warning against those "acting against the interests of the country", which is a tourism and financial services hub.

"Those who have carried out these actions will have to face the very heavy consequences warranted by their anti-patriotic acts," he said in an address to the nation.

Protesters burned tyres and blocked ‌roads as the unrest escalated over the weekend, with police stations and other public infrastructure properties being vandalised.

The mayhem prompted the closure of schools and public transport, with foreign embassies issuing alerts warning its nationals to be cautious.

Despite the curfew, police said there had been several incidents overnight and some arrests.

But the police assured people that by Wednesday morning traffic was again moving throughout the island and said people should resume their normal activities.

When protests over the shortage of water initially started, the government had responded proactively by providing more water to households, according to Zoë McCathie, an analyst at South Africa-based Signal Risk.

The escalation had presented a more "unusual situation for the country's security situation", with the government resorting to closing schools and imposing a curfew, she told the BBC's Newsday programme.

"Protests to this scale and to this extent haven't been seen… since around 1999. So the government's response to this in that case is logical and is necessary," she said.

While the government had managed to "curtail the worst of the unrest" there was still a possibility that protests could return in some areas, with water shortages expected to persist until the rainy season in December, she said.

The cabinet is due to meet on Wednesday afternoon to reassess the situation and decide on the next steps.

articles.title: ‘Very risky choice’: Italy's Meloni warns US-Russia diesel deal could help fund war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday criticised the United States' agreement with Russia on diesel supplies, calling it a “very risky
articles.body: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday criticised the United States' agreement with Russia on diesel supplies, calling it a “very risky choice” that could undermine efforts to bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table over the war in Ukraine.Speaking in the Italian parliament ahead of a European Union summit this week, Meloni said the agreement could provide Moscow with additional revenue to fund the war and weaken the impact of sanctions imposed over its invasion of Ukraine, according to Reuters.“The outcome of this decision is uncertain, while the risks are clear,” she said.“It provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions,” Meloni added.The United States and Russia said last week they had agreed on an initial supply of more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets.US President Donald Trump has defended the arrangement, saying it would help bring down energy prices for American consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.Meloni calls for EU representative in Russia-Ukraine negotiationsMeloni also urged the 27-member European Union to appoint an authoritative representative to negotiate on its behalf over the Russia-Ukraine war.She did not rule out giving a formal mandate to the E3 group, comprising France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to represent the bloc in such discussions.“If France, Germany, and Great Britain believe they can do better on their own than we could all do together, and so far that is the choice they have made, then at least let them do so on behalf of everyone and with an official mandate,” Meloni said, according to Reuters.Her remarks come ahead of an EU summit at which support for Ukraine, including its war funding, is expected to be a key issue. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Sunday that Ukraine's financing would be “front and centre” at the meeting.Trump defends diesel deal as Ukraine objectsTrump has defended the agreement on the grounds of American interests, arguing that increased supplies would ease fuel prices. In a post on his Truth Social platform, he said he had made the right choice for Americans, while also accusing the media of overlooking European payments to Russia for energy.Russian deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said Moscow could supply as much as 3.5 million tonnes of diesel a month to global markets by the end of the year.The arrangement has drawn criticism from Ukraine, which has argued that additional Russian petroleum revenues could help fund Moscow's war effort. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the proposed suspension of sanctions on Russian oil products until April 2027 would undermine Ukraine's efforts to restrict Russia's income from energy exports.“Gifts to Putin will not lead to peace,” Zelenskyy said on Saturday. He added that easing sanctions without a clear and lasting agreement to de-escalate the conflict would be “an obvious sign of weakness”.The EU, meanwhile, has continued to pursue economic pressure on Moscow. The bloc announced a fresh sanctions package targeting individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial network.The contrasting approaches to Russian energy supplies have exposed differences between Washington and European governments over how to pressure Moscow and pursue an end to the war in Ukraine.You use AI every day. articles.title: Delhi protest: Journalists slapped with SC/ST Act for casteist slur against ACP on duty
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) in Delhi has accused a woman journalist and two others of making casteist remarks against him,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) in Delhi has accused a woman journalist and two others of making casteist remarks against him, publicly humiliating him and obstructing his official duties during a protest in the national capital on October 3.The FIR was registered on October 13 at Parliament Street Police Station on the complaint of ACP Vivek Bhagat, who is posted in the Connaught Place subdivision. Journalist Rosy, Gajendra Singh, who is associated with a news portal, and an unidentified person have been named as accused.The case has been registered under Sections 221, 356(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), along with provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.Bhagat has been at the centre of allegations of harassment of women protesters during the recent agitation against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Those allegations are being investigated by the Crime Branch.What the ACP allegedAccording to Bhagat's complaint, the incident took place at Buta Singh Roundabout on October 3, when police personnel were deployed to manage a protest called by Neha Bora and others against the Election Commission of India (ECI).The ACP said the protesters gathered around 2.30 pm and tried to march towards Jantar Mantar. Police personnel announced that restrictions under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) were in force and asked the protesters to disperse. When they allegedly refused to leave, the police began detaining them.Bhagat, who belongs to the Megh/Meghwal Scheduled Caste community, alleged that Rosy made derogatory remarks about his caste after referring to his nameplate. He claimed the remarks were made in the presence of her colleague Gajendra Singh and others.The ACP further alleged that around 3 pm, while he was helping a bus carrying detainees move, Rosy accused him of sexually assaulting her. He claimed that she and her colleagues repeatedly confronted him, questioned his conduct and obstructed him from carrying out his official responsibilities.According to the complaint, Rosy, Singh and others later gathered outside Parliament Street Police Station at around 6.15 pm and staged a protest against him. Bhagat alleged that they raised slogans and portrayed him as a sexual predator and a potential rapist.He also claimed that posts and reels targeting him were subsequently circulated on X and Instagram by the accused and others, including members of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP).Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Six Flags rider who fell to his death was in remission from cancer, survived 'crazy' car fire, sister says
articles.summary: Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath roller coaster remains under investigation after Hassan Kariem fell from the 200-foot-tall ride during a park visit.
articles.body: A Georgia man who survived cancer and escaped a "crazy" car fire just a month ago died after falling from a Six Flags roller coaster, leaving his heartbroken sister struggling to comprehend how her brother could survive so much, only to lose his life in a tragic amusement park accident. Hassan Kariem, 42, died Monday after falling from the 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. His sister, Andrea Clark, 35, told the New York Post on Tuesday that her brother had been in remission from cancer since 2015 and had survived a car fire just weeks before his death. "He's an amazing person," Clark told the outlet through tears. "The coolest part about me was him." MAN DIES AFTER FALLING FROM GOLIATH ROLLER COASTER AT SIX FLAGS OVER GEORGIA Clark, who described her brother as "my hero," called his sudden death "unfair," saying she could not understand how someone who had overcome so much could be gone. "He had other issues, but he's healthy, he was able-bodied. I don't understand it," she said. Clark also recalled her brother's devotion to his loved ones, telling the Post that he worked hard to provide for his family and helped raise his fiancée's daughter, whom he had known since she was 3 years old. "He could do it all," she said. The grieving sister also condemned the circulation of disturbing images showing her brother's final moments as he fell from the roller coaster, urging people to stop sharing them. "That's just evil," Clark told the Post. "It's tragic, and I feel like we've gone too far as a society." ATTORNEY SAYS FATAL SIX FLAGS ROLLER COASTER ACCIDENT COULD RAISE BROADER SAFETY QUESTIONS AS 9 RIDES CLOSE Witnesses described a horrifying scene as Kariem reportedly fell from the ride, with one parkgoer telling local outlet WXIA that the victim appeared in a souvenir photo taken during the roller coaster's run. "He was in our pictures," the witness said. "He fell and hit the car three different times." The Goliath hypercoaster reaches speeds of up to 70 mph and features a 170-foot initial drop, a second 175-foot drop and a 540-degree spiral, according to the park's website. Atlanta Public Schools confirmed Tuesday that Kariem worked for the district as an IT manager and extended its condolences to his family. Six Flags said it was cooperating with authorities investigating the incident and temporarily closed similar roller coasters at other parks across the country as a precaution. articles.title: Hidden video recording device found in cabin of Australian navy ship
articles.summary: Australia's military confirms the device had been discovered, after a senator reports being contacted with allegations of concealed cameras on the ship.
articles.body:
A hidden video recording device has been found in an Australian navy ship's cabin, the Australian Defence Force (ADF) has confirmed.

The device was located on Sunday in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin in Cairns, Queensland.

The confirmation came after independent Australian senator Jacqui Lambie, a former veteran and defence advocate, told parliament she was contacted by personnel with allegations that "concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors' showers facilities".

Australia's defence department has not said whether the device was found in a female-only space and said the incident was referred to the Joint Military Police United.

Lambie told the Australian Senate on Wednesday: "I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered.

"How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask navy."

Later on Wednesday, the defence department confirmed it became aware of a video recording device being found in a HMAS Leeuwin cabin but did not give specific details on where it was discovered.

"Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form," the department said in its statement.

"The ship remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship's crew. The welfare of individuals remains Defence's priority, and support is ongoing.

"As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time."

articles.title: Iraq’s PM tells Saudi crown prince Iraqi territory will not be used for attacks
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones last month in an attack that originated in Iraq.
articles.body:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi has assured Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) that he will not allow Iraqi territory to be used to launch attacks against Saudi Arabia, the Iraqi News Agency (INA) has reported.

Al-Zaidi arrived in Riyadh on Wednesday for his first visit to the kingdom since taking office in May.

He also said he would not allow attacks against other regional countries to be launched from Iraq.

“Iraq’s firm position is not to allow its territory to be used as a launching pad for any attacks or actions that affect the security of the kingdom and the countries of the region, and to be keen on adhering to the principles of good neighbourliness and respecting the sovereignty of Iraq and brotherly and friendly countries,” Al-Zaidi’s office said in a statement, cited by INA.

Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones last month during the Houthis’ lightning offensive in Yemen.

The attack forced Riyadh to temporarily shut down the export route, which Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

The pipeline, which has a maximum capacity of seven million barrels per day, has since resumed operations.

Saudi Arabia said the drone attack originated in Iraq. Baghdad conducted its own investigation and concluded that the strikes were launched from Iraqi territory.

There was no claim of responsibility for the attack, but Iraq is home to numerous Iran-backed armed groups.

articles.title: AMB GORDON SONDLAND: Threading the needle on Ukraine, Russia and China
articles.summary: Trump's Ukraine strategy aims to reshape the global chessboard against China, but Volodymyr Zelensky must adapt his approach to survive it.
articles.body: Let’s get the preliminaries out of the way. Ukraine has corruption problems and political dysfunction of its own. But, in this war, Ukraine is unequivocally the good guy. Russia’s invasion was unprovoked, unjustified and indefensible. Vladimir Putin is the aggressor. Volodymyr Zelensky is defending his country. Period. Now let’s talk about geopolitical reality. Donald Trump is attempting something far more ambitious than ending the war in Ukraine. He is trying to rearrange the strategic chessboard for the next several decades. Understanding that objective is essential to understanding his seemingly contradictory decisions. The United States has one truly consequential long-term strategic competitor: China. Russia is dangerous, nuclear-armed and capable of wreaking havoc on its neighbors. But, Russia is also a declining power with an economy dependent on natural resources, deteriorating demographics and ambitions that, while unacceptable, are largely regional. China is something else entirely. Beijing seeks to challenge American economic, technological and military leadership globally. It has the industrial capacity, financial resources and strategic patience to pursue that ambition for generations. China’s challenge is in a different category altogether. CHINA’S LONG-TERM FINANCES ARE ALL WET AS BILL TO MAINTAIN HUGE NAVY COMES DUE IN 2031 Here is Trump’s dilemma: Europe is not yet strong enough to contain Russia without substantial American support. Despite years of promises, too many NATO allies remain dependent on American military capabilities, intelligence, logistics and leadership. Until Europe can handle Russia largely on its own, the United States must continue devoting enormous resources to European security. Every additional weapons system, dollar and hour of strategic attention consumed by Moscow is a resource unavailable for deterring Beijing or addressing other threats around the world. Trump is trying to change that equation. His apparent objective is to create conditions under which Russia can eventually become a more normal, economically engaged country rather than a permanent adversary requiring America’s undivided attention. Think of it as strategic triage. In the long run, we want a fully economically engaged Russia that has something meaningful to lose, but still needs a good kick in the ass from time to time to remind Putin and his successors to stay the hell out of Europe. That is a far better outcome than a permanently isolated, militarized Russia driven ever deeper into China’s embrace. NATO'S EASTERN FLANK RACES TO REARM AS TRUMP PRESSURE EXPOSES WESTERN EUROPE'S DEFENSE GAP That doesn’t mean trusting Putin. It means understanding his incentives. Putin wants two things: money and real estate. He wants the economic benefits of international engagement and the territorial advantages of empire. Trump is uniquely positioned to offer the former while making the latter prohibitively expensive. That is the needle Trump is trying to thread. But, he is threading it while balancing competing global equities: keeping energy prices manageable, maintaining pressure on Iran, deterring China, supporting Israel, reassuring allies and protecting the American economy. Europe’s continued military dependence makes every calculation harder. And until Europe is genuinely capable of assuming primary responsibility for its own defense, America cannot simply disengage from Russia, however much we might wish to concentrate our resources elsewhere. Which brings us to Zelensky. I have enormous respect for his courage and determination. And when Ukraine strikes Russian oil refineries, the military logic is obvious. Petroleum revenues finance Putin’s war machine. Disrupting them is a legitimate strategic objective when conducted within the laws of war. Zelensky is right to hit Russia where it hurts. But being right is not always enough. An attack that makes perfect sense to Ukrainian military planners may complicate Trump’s larger negotiations, disrupt energy markets and create political problems at home. Zelensky’s first responsibility is Ukraine’s survival. Trump’s first responsibility is America’s interests. Those interests overlap enormously, but they are not identical. Here is what Zelensky must understand: Trump is not simply Ukraine’s principal supplier of weapons, intelligence and money. He is a strategic partner managing a far larger set of global obligations. Zelensky needs to stop approaching Washington principally with a shopping list and start asking a different question: Mr. President, what can Ukraine do to help you accomplish your broader objectives while protecting our sovereignty? TRUMP CALLS FOR UKRAINE TO REPLACE ZELENSKYY AFTER CLASH OVER RUSSIA DIESEL DEAL: 'GET A NEW PRESIDENT' That is not capitulation. It is sophisticated diplomacy. It means coordinating major military and economic initiatives before they become surprises. It means understanding American energy concerns and domestic political pressures. It means offering Trump practical ways to demonstrate progress rather than simply demanding more assistance. And it means recognizing that Trump’s ability to sustain American support depends partly on convincing Americans that his policies are working. There is another reality diplomats often prefer not to discuss: Donald Trump conducts foreign policy through personal relationships to an extraordinary degree. I worked for him. I know. The conventional diplomatic playbook emphasizes prepared meetings, formal communications and bureaucratic coordination. Trump places enormous weight on personal access and whether someone understands what he is trying to achieve. The late diplomat George Ball captured an enduring truth: "Nothing propinks like propinquity." In plain English, proximity matters. TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Zelensky needs to be talking to Trump constantly. Not once a month. Not only when he needs another weapons package. Almost every day. Sometimes to discuss the battlefield. Sometimes to share intelligence. Sometimes to float an idea. Sometimes just to tell him a joke or share some gossip. That may sound trivial when thousands are dying in Ukraine, but it isn’t. Personal familiarity creates trust. Trust creates access. Access creates influence. Even Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with their almost hourly access to Trump, can occasionally be surprised by a decision. That is the nature of his unusually fluid, personalized decision-making process. Imagine the disadvantage of a foreign leader relying exclusively on traditional diplomatic channels. Zelensky cannot afford that disadvantage. There is also the uncomfortable matter of American politics. Trump needs Republicans to retain control of the Senate in November. Zelensky needs Ukraine to survive the coming winter. To a neutral observer, those objectives are hardly equivalent. To each leader, however, they are critical. Should Zelensky intervene in an American election? Absolutely not. Should he understand Trump’s political pressures and help create conditions under which continued American support becomes easier to defend? Absolutely. There is a world of difference between helping a political party and helping an American president demonstrate that his foreign policy is producing results. Zelensky should be looking for opportunities to do the latter every day. Understanding Trump’s political constraints is not the same as surrendering Ukraine’s interests. It is recognizing that the most effective way to secure American support is to make Ukraine’s success part of Trump’s success. But this bargain must run both ways. Zelensky cannot be expected to restrain attacks on Russian energy infrastructure while Putin continues pounding Ukraine’s power plants, cities and civilian infrastructure. Ukraine has already demonstrated a willingness to consider reciprocal restraint. That willingness must be met by Russian action, not simply another American request for Ukrainian patience. If Trump wants Zelensky to accommodate his broader strategy, Trump must use America’s enormous economic leverage to make Putin accommodate it as well. That means no unilateral rewards for aggression, no permanent sanctions relief in exchange for temporary gestures and no settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless while Russia rearms. A temporary diesel arrangement or sanctions reprieve is not normalization. It is a tactic. Real normalization requires verifiable Russian behavior and meaningful consequences for renewed aggression. Putin wants economic engagement. Trump controls much of what makes that engagement possible. That leverage should be used to secure lasting concessions, not exchanged for another fleeting promise. Meanwhile, Europe must accelerate its military transformation. The United States cannot indefinitely remain Europe’s principal insurance policy while simultaneously preparing for the far greater strategic challenge posed by China. The ultimate prize is not a handshake with Putin or another White House announcement. It is a Europe capable of defending itself, a Russia with powerful incentives to stay within its borders and an America free to concentrate its strategic weight where the greatest long-term danger lies. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Until Europe reaches that point, Trump must balance competing military, economic and political demands that Zelensky cannot afford to ignore. And Trump must recognize that Ukraine’s survival is essential to making his larger strategy credible. Zelensky needs Trump’s leverage, weapons and economic power. Trump needs Zelensky’s cooperation to produce a sustainable settlement rather than a theatrical one. Putin must understand he cannot play them against each other indefinitely. The message to Zelensky is simple: Help Trump succeed in his larger geopolitical mission, and insist that Ukraine’s survival be part of that success. The message to Trump is equally simple: Give Zelensky a reason to trust that helping you will not cost him his country. Neither man needs to abandon his interests. Both need to understand the other’s. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That is how transactional diplomacy works when it works well. And that is how you thread the needle. articles.title: Sherrod Brown's 1971 letter argued against releasing Vietnam War POWs, podcast hosts reveal
articles.summary: Sherrod Brown's 1971 letter argued against releasing Vietnam War POWs, raising questions about the Ohio Senate nominee's long-held political views.
articles.body: The Ruthless Podcast hosts surfaced a striking letter to the editor from Ohio Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown arguing against releasing the American Prisoners of War (POWs) during the Vietnam War. "When you think of this disease that’s infected the Democratic Party, you think about [Michigan Democratic Senate Nominee Abdul] El Sayed," podcast co-host Michael Duncan said. "You think of [New York Democratic congressional Darializa Avila] Chevalier, who said she's basically against Western civilization. But Sherrod Brown's been on this his entire career." In the summer of 1971, Brown wrote a letter to the editor published in the News-Journal. The longtime politician, who first ran for office over fifty years ago, asked if the North Vietnamese "released our POWs, what would stop the U.S. from bombing Hanoi and Haiphong?" FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE Brown’s left-wing writings made headlines in 2015 when BuzzFeed reported that the teenager wrote that the Nixon administration was turning the country into a "fascist police-state." Fox News Digital reached out to the Brown campaign for comment and hasn’t received any response. Podcast co-host Comfortably Smug, a noted fan of President Richard Nixon, asserted that it is emotional seeing the footage of President Richard Nixon meeting with the POWs when they returned stateside. TODAY’S LEFTISTS ARE DANGEROUSLY WRONG ABOUT COMMUNISM. JUST LISTEN TO THE SURVIVORS "There's incredible footage, I invite everyone to go see, of when President Nixon brought these POWs home," Smug said. "You hear stories of what it meant to those families to get their loved ones back who were being tortured. You have this guy who is currently running for Senate in this day and age who wrote, he hopes American POWs do not return from being tortured. How is he on the ballot?" With Republicans holding a 53-47 advantage over Democrats in the Senate, Democrats view Ohio as a prime pickup opportunity en route to flipping the chamber. Fox News has classified Brown’s showdown with incumbent Senator Jon Husted as a "toss-up." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE While critics may dismiss the discovery of these op-eds as being outdated or another example of political rhetoric during campaign season, podcast co-host John Ashbrook noted how it suggests where Brown’s sympathies lie. "If you live in the state of Ohio, or you're a political junkie like us, you've heard it said over and over again, ‘Oh, Sherrod Brown is a crazy lefty,’" Cincinnati native John Ashbrook said. "It's sort of dismissed. He's a lefty, and nobody ever fills in the gaps. Well, I think this piece that he wrote in the 70s sort of explains why a lot of people were like maybe he is sort of sympathetic to the communists." Brown previously served three terms in the U.S. Senate representing Ohio from 2007 to 2025. articles.title: Search for missing dog in Yellowstone is under pressure as winter nears
articles.summary: A small dog that's been on the loose in Yellowstone National Park for a month has been spotted crossing intersections, strolling through employee housing and entering lodges through automatic doors.
articles.body: A small dog that's been on the loose in Yellowstone National Park for a month has been spotted crossing intersections, strolling through employee housing and entering lodges through automatic doors. Yet Luna, a Jack Russell terrier from California, has eluded capture. And with winter closing in, volunteers in the search for the dog say its time is running out. Katie Boucher, the volunteer helming the rescue effort, says Luna has good survival instincts. Luna’s family prefers to remain anonymous, but told Boucher that before she was adopted, the 10-year-old dog spent the first year of her life surviving on the streets. So far, temperatures haven't dropped low enough that Luna could freeze, but that could change in an instant. Boucher is hoping the light dusting of snow in the area is enough to make her want to come home. “Hopefully she has decided that winter in Yellowstone National Park is not a good vacation,” Boucher said. An escape into the wilderness On the day she was lost, Luna's family left her in a cabin, with a do-not-disturb sign, while they ventured out to see the park. In what they believe was an accident, housekeeping opened the room door and let Luna out. “The staff then proceeded to chase her around that area of the park for over two hours before the owners came back and discovered all the chaos and their dog missing,” Boucher said. Luna's family searched for their pup, but were told it was likely the terrier either died or was eaten by a coyote, Boucher recounted. Days after leaving Yellowstone, Luna's owners were told she had been spotted, and contacted Boucher, the president of the Norris Ark Training and Recovery Center in Norris, Montana, an area just north of the national park. “I cannot fathom how I would feel if I had been taking the vacation of a lifetime, and looking for all these memorable experiences in one of the most beautiful places on earth, and lost one of my family members there,” Boucher said. Boucher has been tracking sightings of Luna and says the dog is retracing her family's steps from the day before she was lost, sneaking into eateries or lodges they had visited. Locals and tourists calling Luna’s name or chasing her trigger her fight-or-flight response and drive the dog further into the park, Boucher said. The volunteers set a humane trap to lure Luna in using the scent of her family, since using food could attract other wildlife like bears. Time is running out as winter closes in This might be the last week Boucher will be able to look for Luna, as weather could potentially limit how long she can stay in the park. Right now, she's sleeping at an RV park for seasonal employees that closes next Monday. Afterward, she'll have to look for somewhere else to stay. Despite the time crunch, she's confident she's close to returning Luna to her family. “Her behavior pattern suggests to me that she is looking for her family,” Boucher said. The search for the small pup has rallied locals and tourists visiting the area. Marie Jaskula, a resident in the area that runs one of the park's general stores, has posted signs at every entrance to the park so visitors can look out for Luna too. “It’s really hard to stress the importance of do not chase,” said Jaskula. “Everybody sees this little dog buzz across the intersection or maybe around their employee housing, and the first instinct is to call her name and chase her.”

articles.body: NEW DELHI: With CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka in Tihar Jail, party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Wednesday called for a 'Tricolour march' at Delhi’s Connaught Place on Friday, challenging the police action against the activists.In a video posted on X, Dipke asked people to assemble at Central Park in Connaught Place at 5pm on October 16, carrying the national flag. articles.title: Starlink row: Govt set to examine satellite internet, says parliamentary panel chief Nishikant Dubey
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The government is set to discuss satellite internet services in the coming days, with a parliamentary panel selecting the subject for a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The government is set to discuss satellite internet services in the coming days, with a parliamentary panel selecting the subject for a detailed examination amid the ongoing row over Elon Musk's allegations that powerful business interests are obstructing Starlink's entry into India.BJP MP Nishikant Dubey, chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology, said the panel would take up the issue at its upcoming meeting. “We will discuss the satellite net issue at our meeting in the coming days,” Dubey told PTI after a meeting of the panel.A threadbare examination, in parliamentary parlance, refers to a detailed and comprehensive scrutiny of an issue, including its regulatory, commercial and security implications.The panel's decision comes amid a public exchange between Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX, which operates Starlink, and Indian political and business figures over the company's pending approval to launch satellite internet services in the country.In a series of posts on X last week, Musk targeted Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, with sarcastic jabs. Musk also alleged that some business groups were attempting to maintain a “monopolistic chokehold” over Indian consumers.The ministry of communications has rejected the allegations, describing suggestions that India's regulatory framework or its implementation was unfair or discriminatory as “baseless” and “misconceived”. The government has maintained that satellite operators must meet the same regulatory requirements, including security conditions and spectrum allocation rules, before commencing commercial services.Dubey had earlier hit back at Musk over the Starlink controversy, asserting that India would not change its security policy under pressure or in response to social media posts.In a post on X on Sunday, Dubey alleged that Starlink's entry raised challenges for India's security agencies and said the parliamentary committee had examined the concerns faced by them.“The ministry of defence, the ministry of home affairs, and our investigation agencies are being affected by the dangerous games of these threats,” Dubey wrote.He also claimed that the government led by former prime minister Manmohan Singh had alerted the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) to such threats in 2013-14.Urging Musk to focus on making internet services affordable in the United States before criticising India, Dubey had said, “India is a healthy democratic, sovereign nation; it does not change its security policy under pressure or social media.”He further argued that financial considerations alone would not determine the government's decision on Starlink, writing: “If our policy were driven by money, we would have rolled out the red carpet welcome for you despite opposition from the security agencies.”Musk, meanwhile, has argued that Starlink's entry would increase competition and expand consumer choice. articles.title: Burnham - Rosebank and Jackdaw decisions coming 'shortly'
articles.summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to stop "faffing about" with the North Sea oil and gas fields.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said a decision on whether to give the go-ahead to two oil and gas fields will be made "shortly".

Parties at Westminster are calling for Burnham to approve plans for Rosebank, an oil field off Shetland, and gas field Jackdaw, east of Aberdeen.

The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government.

Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged Burnham "to stop faffing about" when it comes to the North Sea drilling.

She said: "In July, he said he would approve the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields in the North Sea. What's he waiting for?

"If he'd approved them back then, we would have British gas warming British homes this winter.

"All of the gas from Jackdaw goes onto the British grid, so will we now stop faffing about and approve Rosebank and Jackdaw?"

Jackdaw, which is about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months.

Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas.

The prime minister responded: "She asked me what I'm waiting for – I've had to wait for the government process, which was struck down by the courts under the Conservative government, to be fixed because they messed it up, and we inherited that situation.

"So I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas, we will set out our decisions shortly."

Licences for the fields were granted by the Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe.

They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs.

Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply.

Burnham has previously left open the possibility of granting approval to Jackdaw and Rosebank.

However he has said he will stick to Labour's promise not to issue new oil and gas licences while honouring existing ones.

It is not yet known when the government will announce its decision.

articles.title: Deja Vu: Dancing with Pussycat Dolls on tour was surreal
articles.summary: The band says: "Nicole did tell us that she was proud of us."
articles.body:
A girl group that toured Europe with The Pussycat Dolls said it was 'surreal' to join their childhood heroes on stage.

Deja Vu, formed of Elle Botterill and Tyrece Lewis from Buckinghamshire alongside Venezuelan-born Carolina Diaz, performed their first-ever live shows during the 20-date arena tour across the UK and Europe.

The group were left stunned when Kimberly Wyatt personally invited them to join the headliners during the dance break of their hit song, Buttons.

Botterill said: "Even afterwards, we were just like, 'I can't believe that's actually just happened, we've been on stage dancing with The Pussycat Dolls in front of thousands of people'."

The PCD Forever Tour, celebrating the 20th anniversary of The Pussycat Dolls, saw the trio visit cities including Prague and Paris, before finishing at London's O2 on Tuesday.

The group had formed during the Covid-19 pandemic and reached the semi-finals of The Voice UK in 2023, but the tour was the first time they had performed full shows for an audience.

Lewis said: "We were genuinely thrown in at the deep end, we went from dancing for social media videos on street corners to swimming with great whites.

Diaz added: "I'm not going to lie, we did have a bit of imposter syndrome at the first shows.

"But it taught us that we are capable and deserving of these things after working so hard for all them years."

Now, the group will focus on their own original music ahead of their debut headline show on 1 December at The Grace in London.

For the trio, who grew up as massive fans of the American pop group, the entire tour served as a masterclass.

Lewis beamed: "Nicole did tell us that she was proud of us... That is everything to us."

Botterill laughed: "I almost cried big girl tears... I'm going to get it tattooed across my chest!"
